mathleague-2004-05-g4-01.title: Change into dimes
mathleague-2004-05-g4-01.body:
\$1 is the same as 10 dimes, and each gumball costs 1 dime, so I can buy 10 gumballs.

**Answer: (C) 10**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-02.title: Zero factor
mathleague-2004-05-g4-02.body:
If 0 is one of the factors, the whole product is 0.

**Answer: (A) 0**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-03.title: Multiply
mathleague-2004-05-g4-03.body:
A week has 7 days, so Ork delivers $2 \times 7 = 14$ babies.

**Answer: (C) 14**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-03.title: Count by twos
mathleague-2004-05-g4-03.body:
2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 — one number for each of the 7 days.

**Answer: (C) 14**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-04.title: Work in order
mathleague-2004-05-g4-04.body:
2 more than 52 is 54, and 5 less than 54 is 49.

**Answer: (B) 49**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-04.title: Combine the changes
mathleague-2004-05-g4-04.body:
Adding 2 and taking away 5 is the same as taking away 3: $52 - 3 = 49$.

**Answer: (B) 49**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-05.title: Count back
mathleague-2004-05-g4-05.body:
One day before Monday is Sunday, and two days before Monday is Saturday.

**Answer: (A) Saturday**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-05.title: List the week
mathleague-2004-05-g4-05.body:
Saturday, Sunday, Monday: Saturday comes two days before Monday.

**Answer: (A) Saturday**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-06.title: Add and subtract separately
mathleague-2004-05-g4-06.body:
The added numbers are $15+13+11+9+7+5 = 60$; the subtracted numbers are $14+12+10+8+6+4 = 54$. So the result is $60 - 54 = 6$.

**Answer: (A) 6**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-07.title: Split 45 minutes
mathleague-2004-05-g4-07.body:
45 minutes = 15 + 30 minutes. 15 minutes after 4:45 is 5:00, and 30 minutes later it is 5:30.

**Answer: (D) 5:30**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-07.title: Add minutes
mathleague-2004-05-g4-07.body:
$45 + 45 = 90$ minutes past 4:00, which is 1 hour 30 minutes past 4:00, or 5:30.

**Answer: (D) 5:30**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-08.title: Count all pennies
mathleague-2004-05-g4-08.body:
The left side is $200 + 20 = 220$ pennies. Taking away 1 dollar (100 pennies) leaves $220 - 100 = 120$ pennies.

**Answer: (B) 120**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-09.title: Undo the multiplication
mathleague-2004-05-g4-09.body:
Dividing by 205 undoes one multiplication by 205: $(205 \times 205) \div 205 = 205$.

**Answer: (D) 205**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-10.title: Radius is half the diameter
mathleague-2004-05-g4-10.body:
The radius is half of the diameter: $16 \div 2 = 8$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 8**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-10.title: Picture it
mathleague-2004-05-g4-10.body:
The diameter goes all the way across the wheel through the center; the radius goes only from the center to the edge, which is half of the way: 8 cm.

**Answer: (B) 8**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-12.title: Write it out
mathleague-2004-05-g4-12.body:
Ten thousand is written 10 000, which has 4 zeros.

**Answer: (B) 4**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-12.title: Use powers of ten
mathleague-2004-05-g4-12.body:
Ten is 10 (one 0), one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000, and ten thousand $= 10 \times 1000 = 10\,000$ adds one more 0, so 4 zeros.

**Answer: (B) 4**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-14.title: Try and check
mathleague-2004-05-g4-14.body:
If each of us put in 4 dimes, the total is $4 \times 4 + 3 = 19$. If each put in 5 dimes, the total is $4 \times 5 + 3 = 23$. That is choice A.

**Answer: (A) 23**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-14.title: Remainder when dividing by 4
mathleague-2004-05-g4-14.body:
The total is (a multiple of 4) + 3, so it leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4. $23 = 4 \times 5 + 3$ works; 24, 25, 26 leave remainders 0, 1, 2.

**Answer: (A) 23**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-15.title: Times 1
mathleague-2004-05-g4-15.body:
$2 - 1 = 1$, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so the answer is $8 - 3 = 5$.

**Answer: (C) 5**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-16.title: Check for even
mathleague-2004-05-g4-16.body:
A number divisible by 6 must be even. 6633 is odd, so it is not divisible by 6.

**Answer: (D) 6633**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-17.title: Find the number
mathleague-2004-05-g4-17.body:
The only number that gives 0 when multiplied by 5 is 0. Then $0 \times 6 = 0$.

**Answer: (A) 0**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-17.title: Think about it
mathleague-2004-05-g4-17.body:
Five times the number is 0, so the number is nothing at all. Six times nothing is still nothing: 0.

**Answer: (A) 0**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-18.title: Same size parts
mathleague-2004-05-g4-18.body:
Both parts are one thousand, and two thousands make 2000.

**Answer: (B) 2000**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-19.title: Divide by 4
mathleague-2004-05-g4-19.body:
A square has 4 equal sides, so each side is $64 \div 4 = 16$.

**Answer: (C) 16**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-19.title: Check the choices
mathleague-2004-05-g4-19.body:
Side 16 gives perimeter $4 \times 16 = 64$. Side 8 gives only 32, and side 32 gives 128.

**Answer: (C) 16**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-20.title: Look at the two folds
mathleague-2004-05-g4-20.body:
Folding a square along a diagonal gives two triangles; folding it through the middle of two opposite sides gives two rectangles. Triangles and rectangles are both polygons. So only squares are impossible.

**Answer: (D) squares**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-20.title: Why not squares
mathleague-2004-05-g4-20.body:
If the fold goes edge to edge, each half has one side as long as the square but the other side only half as long, so it is a rectangle that is not a square. A diagonal fold gives triangles. So the halves can never be squares.

**Answer: (D) squares**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-21.title: Check the choices
mathleague-2004-05-g4-21.body:
4 and 16 are not divisible by 12. 24 is divisible by both 8 and 12, and 24 is smaller than 48.

**Answer: (C) 24**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-21.title: List multiples
mathleague-2004-05-g4-21.body:
Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, ... 12 is not divisible by 8, but $24 = 3 \times 8$. So 24.

**Answer: (C) 24**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-22.title: Odd times odd
mathleague-2004-05-g4-22.body:
2005 is odd, and an odd number times an odd number is always odd.

**Answer: (C) odd**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-22.title: Test examples
mathleague-2004-05-g4-22.body:
$2005 \times 1 = 2005$, $2005 \times 3 = 6015$: these are not always 2005, not even, and 6015 is not prime (it is divisible by 5). Both are odd, and odd $\times$ odd is always odd.

**Answer: (C) odd**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-23.title: Find the numbers
mathleague-2004-05-g4-23.body:
The only way to write 7 as a product of two different whole numbers is $1 \times 7$. Their sum is $1 + 7 = 8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-23.title: 7 is prime
mathleague-2004-05-g4-23.body:
7 has only the divisors 1 and 7, so the numbers are 1 and 7, and $1 + 7 = 8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-24.title: Use 1
mathleague-2004-05-g4-24.body:
If one number is 1, the product is the other number $n$, but the sum is $n + 1$, which is bigger. So the answer is 1.

**Answer: (A) 1**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-24.title: Test the others
mathleague-2004-05-g4-24.body:
With 2: try $2$ and $2$: sum 4, product 4, not greater. With 3: $3$ and $3$ give sum 6, product 9. With 4: $4$ and $2$ give sum 6, product 8. Only 1 always works.

**Answer: (A) 1**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-25.title: Count letters after
mathleague-2004-05-g4-25.body:
The 25 letters other than the chosen one split as before + after = 25, with before = 4 × after. So after = 5 and before = 20. The letter with 5 letters after it (V, W, X, Y, Z) is U, and 20 letters come before U.

**Answer: (D) U**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-25.title: Check each choice
mathleague-2004-05-g4-25.body:
E: 4 before, 21 after. G: 6 before, 19 after. T: 19 before, 6 after. U: 20 before, 5 after, and $20 = 4 \times 5$.

**Answer: (D) U**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-26.title: Look at the increase
mathleague-2004-05-g4-26.body:
Doubling my nickels added $37 - 22 = 15$¢, which is 3 extra nickels. Doubling adds as many nickels as I already have, so I have 3 nickels.

**Answer: (A) 3**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-26.title: Check
mathleague-2004-05-g4-26.body:
With 3 nickels (15¢) and 7¢ in pennies, I have 22¢. Doubling the nickels gives 6 nickels = 30¢, plus 7¢ = 37¢. ✓

**Answer: (A) 3**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-27.title: Unit price
mathleague-2004-05-g4-27.body:
12 clips for 48¢ means 1 clip costs $48 \div 12 = 4$¢. For \$1 = 100¢ I get $100 \div 4 = 25$ clips.

**Answer: (B) 25**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-27.title: Scale up
mathleague-2004-05-g4-27.body:
48¢ buys 12 clips, so 96¢ buys 24 clips. The extra 4¢ buys one more clip: 25 clips for \$1.

**Answer: (B) 25**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-28.title: Work backwards
mathleague-2004-05-g4-28.body:
Sam bought twice as many as Lee, so Lee bought $18 \div 2 = 9$. Lee bought 3 times as many as Pat, so Pat bought $9 \div 3 = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-28.title: Check forwards
mathleague-2004-05-g4-28.body:
If Pat bought 3, Lee bought $3 \times 3 = 9$ and Sam bought $2 \times 9 = 18$. ✓

**Answer: (B) 3**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-29.title: Same side
mathleague-2004-05-g4-29.body:
The bus and the train are closest when they are on the same side of the vendor. Then they are $5 - 2 = 3$ km apart.

**Answer: (A) 3 km**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-29.title: Both cases
mathleague-2004-05-g4-29.body:
On opposite sides they are $2 + 5 = 7$ km apart; on the same side $5 - 2 = 3$ km. The least is 3 km.

**Answer: (A) 3 km**

mathleague-2004-05-g4-30.title: Count the doublings
mathleague-2004-05-g4-30.body:
From Sunday to Saturday there are 6 days, so the size doubles 6 times: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 times as big.

**Answer: (D) 64**
